content: 1. Alfalfa (Medicago sativa) is used for various conditions, including asthma, arthritis, diabetes, diuresis, hypercholesterolemia, indigestion, and thrombocytopenic purpura. The recommended oral dosage is 5-10 grams three times daily (TID). 2. Alfalfa contains vitamins A, C, E, and K, as well as minerals such as calcium (Ca), potassium (K), phosphorus (P), and iron (Fe). 3. Alfalfa is possibly effective in managing type II hyperlipoproteinemia. 4. Alfalfa and certain medications or supplements, such as aceclofenac, acemetacin, agrimony, alteplase, American ginseng, antithrombin alpha, antithrombin III, argatroban, aspirin (oral and rectal), bemiparin, bivalirudin, celecoxib, choline magnesium trisalicylate, cinnamon, cordyceps, dabigatran, dalteparin, diclofenac, diflunisal, dong quai, enoxaparin, epoprostenol, etodolac, fennel, fenoprofen, feverfew, flurbiprofen, fondaparinux, forskolin, garlic, ginger, ginkgo biloba, heparin, horse chestnut seed, ibuprofen (oral and IV), indomethacin, ketoprofen, ketorolac (oral and intranasal), lornoxicam, meclofenamate, mefenamic acid, meloxicam, nabumetone, naproxen, oxaprozin, Panax ginseng, parecoxib, pau d’arco, phenindione, phytoestrogens, piroxicam, protamine, reishi, reteplase, salicylates (non-ASA), salsalate, Siberian ginseng, sulfasalazine, sulindac, tenecteplase, tolfenamic acid, and tolmetin, all increase anticoagulation. Caution and close monitoring are advised when these are used concurrently with alfalfa. 5. Alfalfa increases the toxicity of chlorpromazine through pharmacodynamic synergism, potentially leading to increased photosensitivity. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear. 6. Alfalfa decreases the effects of mestranol through pharmacodynamic antagonism. This interaction is theoretical, and its clinical significance is unknown. 7. Alfalfa decreases vitamin E levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unclear. 8. Alfalfa may cause photosensitivity, pancytopenia (notably from ground alfalfa seeds), and hypersensitivity reactions. 9. Alfalfa should be avoided prior to surgery due to its potential to increase bleeding risk. 10. The above-ground portion of alfalfa is considered safer than the seeds. 11. Alfalfa’s safety during pregnancy and lactation is not well established. It is categorized as N/A for pregnancy and lactation. However, it is generally considered acceptable, as controlled studies in pregnant women have shown no evidence of fetal risk.
